overview: This 1783 to 1800 atlas record highlights northern Maratha power around Ujjain, Gwalior and the approaches to Delhi. Its broad outline excludes Pune, Dhar and Maheshwar and cannot represent every local ruler’s authority. It is a regional view of several Maratha states and their neighbors, separate from the wider Maratha Confederacy card.

periods.title: Mahadji’s northern power
periods.summary: Mahadji Scindia built a powerful northern state, recruiting Benoit de Boigne to train his armies.

periods.title: Daulat Rao succeeds
periods.summary: Mahadji died in 1794; Daulat Rao inherited his position. The atlas stops before the later Anglo-Maratha wars.

items.text: Ujjain was the Scindias’ chief town during this map interval. A court needed residences, artisans and merchants as well as soldiers. The later move to a new capital at Gwalior in 1810 helps explain why the dynasty is so often associated with Gwalior today.

Mahadji Scindia strengthened his armies by employing the European officer Benoit de Boigne. Training and military organization helped turn a northern Maratha ruling house into a formidable power. Mahadji’s death in 1794 brought Daulat Rao to the throne, rather than ending the state.

Diplomacy generated a mountain of paper. The British Library catalogues hundreds of pages of correspondence between the Bengal government and David Anderson, its agent with Scindia, in 1782 and 1783. These surviving records let historians examine negotiation alongside the much more visible battles.

A small Gwalior rupee complicates a single-color map: a 1781 example carries both a flower and a pistol mark. Numismatic research attributes it to the neighboring Rana of Gohad’s occupation, not Scindia. Tiny symbols can expose changes of government that broad outlines conceal.

Visiting Ujjain in 1792, William Hunter described timber house frames filled with brick, under tiled or terraced roofs. On the paved main bazaar, shops occupied the lower storey and owners lived above. For some shopkeepers, the journey home was simply upstairs.

At Barua Sagar in 1792, Jhansi’s governor Raghunath Hari showed Hunter English books, including an encyclopedia whose illustrations local artists had copied. He wanted a language teacher and received a dictionary. This was an adult ruler’s personal study, not a public school system.

The same governor demonstrated an electrical machine made by a member of his staff. It charged a jar and startled spectators with shocks; he asked how it worked. Hunter’s account catches a small court workshop experimenting with science, not merely collecting impressive objects.

Hunter says Raghunath Hari had visited Kanpur for medical help. At Barua Sagar he offered guests cabbages, lettuce and celery from his garden. One patient’s journey had also become a route for exchanging tastes and plants.

Ujjain’s Maratha-period buildings preserved a lively craft world: woodworkers carved balconies and galleries, while temple paintings brought together artistic influences from Pune, Kangra and Malwa. A decorated balcony was both part of a house and a public display of its makers’ skill.

Ujjain inherited an observatory established earlier by Jai Singh of Jaipur. Its Nadi Valay instrument uses a shadow to tell time, with different faces lit in different seasons. The surviving complex was restored later: scientific heritage accumulated across rulers rather than starting afresh with each dynasty.

Nearby Maheshwar lies outside this atlas outline, but its Holkar court belongs in the regional story. Ahilyabai took power with the Peshwa’s permission in 1767. Her patronage welcomed poets, scholars and craftspeople, and her public audiences provided a place to bring grievances.

Ahilyabai’s projects included wells, tanks, river steps and rest houses along pilgrimage routes. These buildings addressed practical needs as well as religious ones: travelers needed water, places to stop and access to the river. This is evidence of public provision, not of universal household plumbing.

sections.title: A mango dispute, writing and living skills

items.text: A 1787 document from Dhar, just outside the mapped region, concerns a dispute over mango trees in Sahib Rai’s orchard. Anwar Beg and Sayyid Azam withdrew their claim before a judge and local officials. Even an orchard could leave a paper trail lasting centuries.

The Dhar writing sample is fārigh-khaṭṭī, a Persian documentary term used here for a release from a claim. This is the historian’s Roman transcription of the 1787 document, not a reconstruction of its handwritten letters. Its witnesses used both Perso-Arabic and Nagri scripts.

Dhar’s archive also preserves Hindi administrative orders under Maratha rulers, with vocabulary inherited from Persian administration. Government did not operate in only one language. Families guarding property documents could carry records across changes of dynasty, keeping old claims relevant to new officials.

Much later, in a 2020 account from Maheshwar, REHWA described teaching women to weave and running the Ahilya School for weavers’ children. A designer discussed seasonal colors and exchanging ideas with artisans over lunch. This is a modern continuation of regional textile work, not an eighteenth-century classroom.

The year 1800 is an atlas boundary, not the disappearance of the northern states. Wars followed in 1803 to 1805 and 1817 to 1818. At Mahidpur in December 1817, the East India Company’s forces defeated Indore’s army, illustrating how military defeat reshaped regional power.

ending.text: Maratha states continued after this map’s 1800 endpoint. Subsequent Anglo-Maratha wars transformed their independence and relationships with the East India Company. Cities, households, crafts and records outlasted these political changes.
